items.value: Only statements 2 and 4 are correct - the State cannot contract Aadhaar data out to private corporations, and Aadhaar can be required for benefits funded from the Consolidated Fund of India
items.reasoning: In K.S. Puttaswamy (2018) the Supreme Court read down the authentication-data retention rule to six months, not the three months stated, so statement 1 is wrong. Statement 2 follows from the striking down of Section 57 of the Aadhaar Act, which had allowed body corporates and private persons to use Aadhaar for identification; the State can no longer share Aadhaar data with private companies by contract. Statement 3 is wrong for the same reason - the Court held Aadhaar was not mandatory for bank accounts, mobile connections, school admissions or insurance. Statement 4 is the one use the Court expressly upheld: Section 7 permits Aadhaar to be required for subsidies, benefits and services charged to the Consolidated Fund of India.

items.value: The Rajya Sabha has powers equal to the Lok Sabha in amending the Constitution
items.reasoning: Article 368 requires a constitutional amendment Bill to be passed separately by each House by the prescribed special majority, and there is no provision for a joint sitting to resolve a deadlock - so on amendment the two Houses are exactly equal. Creating a new All India Service is not an equal power but a special power of the Rajya Sabha alone, since Article 312 requires its resolution to start the process. Removing the government by a no-confidence motion, and voting demands for grants (and therefore moving cut motions on them), lie exclusively with the Lok Sabha.

items.value: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct; MPLADS funds are non-lapsable, so statement 3 is wrong
items.reasoning: The MPLADS guidelines require the funds to be spent on works creating durable community assets - drinking water, education, public health, sanitation, roads - so statement 1 holds. They also earmark 15 per cent of a member's allocation for areas with Scheduled Caste population and 7.5 per cent for Scheduled Tribe areas, so statement 2 holds. Statement 3 is wrong and is what eliminates option C: MPLADS funds are expressly non-lapsable and an unspent balance is carried forward to the next year. The guidelines further require the District Authority to inspect at least 10 per cent of the works under implementation every year, so statement 4 holds.

items.value: Protection against untouchability falls under the Right to Equality
items.reasoning: Untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form forbidden by Article 17, which sits within Articles 14 to 18 - the group of rights headed Right to Equality. The Right against Exploitation is the nearest distractor but covers different ground: Articles 23 and 24 deal with traffic in human beings, begar and forced labour, and the employment of children in hazardous work.

items.value: Separation of the judiciary from the executive is enjoined by a Directive Principle of State Policy (Article 50)
items.reasoning: Article 50, in Part IV, directs the State to take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State. The Preamble contains no such direction, the Seventh Schedule only distributes legislative subjects between the Union and the States, and the separation is a written constitutional mandate rather than a mere convention.

items.value: The Macro Economic Framework Statement is mandated by the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003
items.reasoning: Section 3 of the FRBM Act, 2003 obliges the Central Government to lay before both Houses, along with the Budget, the Macro-Economic Framework Statement, the Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement and the Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement. It is therefore a statutory requirement, not a convention. Article 112 deals with the Annual Financial Statement and Article 110(1) defines a Money Bill; Article 113 deals with demands for grants - none of them mentions these statements.

items.value: A constitutional government is by definition a limited government
items.reasoning: Constitutionalism means government bound by a higher law: the Constitution both confers and confines the powers of every organ of the State, so that power is exercised within defined limits and subject to checks. A government may be popular, multi-party, or dominated by its legislature and still be arbitrary; what makes it constitutional is precisely that its authority is limited.

items.value: The Preamble, the Directive Principles and the Fundamental Duties all reflect the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
items.reasoning: The Preamble's promise of justice, liberty, equality, fraternity and the dignity of the individual restates the opening ideals of the UDHR. The Directive Principles carry its economic, social and cultural rights - the right to work, to a living wage, to education, to public assistance and to health - which the Fundamental Rights do not cover. The Fundamental Duties answer to Article 29(1) of the UDHR, which declares that everyone has duties to the community; that link is the judgement call in the item, since the Duties were inserted in 1976 on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee, but the parallel with Article 29 is a real one, and only option D includes all three.

items.value: Statements 1 and 2 are correct - free legal aid on the ground of income turns on being below the prescribed ceiling, and not all senior citizens qualify
items.reasoning: Section 12 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 gives free legal services to listed classes - members of Scheduled Castes and Tribes, women and children, persons with disabilities, industrial workmen, persons in custody, victims of trafficking or of mass disaster - and otherwise to any person whose annual income is below the prescribed ceiling, which NALSA generally puts at Rs 1,00,000, so statement 1 stands. Statement 4 is wrong because age by itself confers no entitlement: a senior citizen must still satisfy one of the statutory grounds, and the statement is unconditional. Statement 3 is wrong because Other Backward Classes are not a listed class and no Rs 3,00,000 ceiling applies to them. Statement 2 is the weak link and is accepted here largely because the other two fail; the income ceilings are in any case set by the State Governments and vary, so no single national figure is beyond argument. Option C is the runner-up.

items.value: Only pairs 1 and 3 are correctly matched - Alma-Ata with healthcare and Talanoa Dialogue with climate change
items.reasoning: The Alma-Ata Declaration of 1978 proclaimed Health for All through primary health care, so pair 1 is right; the Talanoa Dialogue was the facilitative dialogue launched at COP23 under the UNFCCC to take stock of collective climate action, so pair 3 is right. The Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907 codified the laws and customs of war - biological and chemical weapons are governed by the Biological Weapons Convention of 1972 and the Chemical Weapons Convention of 1993 - so pair 2 is wrong. The Under2 Coalition is the Under 2 Degrees group of states and regions pledging deep emission cuts; it has nothing to do with child rights, so pair 4 is wrong.

items.value: In a parliamentary system the Government is responsible to Parliament and can be removed by it
items.reasoning: The defining feature of a parliamentary executive is the collective responsibility of the council of ministers to the legislature: the government holds office only so long as it commands the confidence of the popular House and falls when that confidence is withdrawn. Option A describes a national or all-party government, option C describes a directly elected executive answerable to the voters, and option D describes a fixed-term presidential-style executive that Parliament cannot dismiss.

items.value: The Directive Principles of State Policy declare the ideal of a Welfare State
items.reasoning: The welfare-state programme is spelt out in Part IV: Article 38 requires the State to secure a social order in which justice informs all institutions of national life, Article 39 speaks of adequate means of livelihood and the distribution of material resources for the common good, and Articles 41 to 43 promise work, education, public assistance and a living wage. The Preamble sets out ideals without prescribing this programme, and the Fundamental Rights operate mainly as restraints on State action rather than as positive obligations of welfare.

items.value: Only statement 2 is correct - judicial review is provided for, but the Constitution nowhere defines a 'basic structure'
items.reasoning: The expression basic structure appears nowhere in the Constitution. It is a doctrine evolved by the Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and filled out case by case since, which is why the Court has never given an exhaustive list of its contents - so statement 1 is wrong. Judicial review, by contrast, is expressly provided for: Article 13 makes laws inconsistent with the Fundamental Rights void, and Articles 32 and 226 arm the Supreme Court and the High Courts to enforce them, so statement 2 is correct.

items.value: Gandhism and Marxism agree on the final goal of a stateless society
items.reasoning: Both look forward to a society in which the coercive state has disappeared: Marx to the withering away of the state once the classless society is reached, Gandhi to an enlightened anarchy of self-governing village republics in which the individual is his own ruler. They part company on everything else - Gandhi rejected class struggle in favour of trusteeship and class harmony, opposed the forcible abolition of private property, and denied that economic forces determine the course of history.

items.value: The bureaucracy is an agency for the implementation of public policy
items.reasoning: The civil service is the permanent executive: policy is framed by the political executive and the legislature, and the bureaucracy's defining function is to carry it out. The other three describe consequences to which bureaucratic action may contribute but which do not define the institution - widening democracy, strengthening federalism and securing political stability are the work of representative and constitutional institutions, not of the civil service as such.

items.value: The Preamble is a part of the Constitution but has no legal effect independently of the other parts
items.reasoning: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) the Supreme Court held that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution, overruling the contrary view taken in the Berubari Union reference. But it is neither a source of power nor a source of prohibition, and it is not enforceable in a court by itself; its use is to resolve ambiguity in the provisions that follow. That is exactly the position option D states. Option C overstates it by putting the Preamble on a par with the enforceable articles, and options A and B understate it.

items.value: Gold Tranche (Reserve Tranche) is a credit facility granted by the IMF to its members
items.reasoning: A member pays part of its IMF quota in foreign currency or SDRs rather than in its own currency, and that portion is the reserve tranche, historically the gold tranche. The member may draw up to it automatically and without conditionality, because in substance it is drawing on its own reserves held with the Fund. It is not a World Bank lending window, has nothing to do with the WTO, and is not an operation of a domestic central bank.

items.value: Statements 2 and 3 are correct - the Directive Principles are not enforceable by any court but are to guide the State in making laws
items.reasoning: Article 37 says the provisions of Part IV shall not be enforceable by any court, but that they are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply them in making laws. Statement 2 is a direct restatement of the first half of that Article and statement 3 of the second half, so both are correct. Statement 1 asserts the exact opposite of statement 2 and is therefore wrong.

items.value: Only statement 1 is correct - a non-member may be a Minister for six months, but conviction does not bring a permanent electoral disqualification
items.reasoning: Article 164(4) allows a person who is not a member of the State Legislature to hold ministerial office, but only for six consecutive months, after which he ceases to be a Minister unless he is elected in the meantime - which is the substance of statement 1. Statement 2 is clearly wrong: Section 8(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 disqualifies a convicted person from the date of conviction and for a further six years from release, a fixed period and not a permanent bar. Note that statement 1 is loosely worded - being eligible to vote (18 years) is not by itself sufficient, because Article 173 requires a person to be at least 25 to be a member of a Legislative Assembly and the courts have held a Minister must be qualified for membership. On that strict reading of the words as printed the answer would be D, and that is the runner-up here; the answer given takes the phrase as identifying an ordinary citizen rather than as stating the qualifying condition.

items.value: Statements 1 and 3 are correct - the President may summon Parliament at any place, and no minimum number of sitting days is prescribed
items.reasoning: Article 85(1) empowers the President to summon each House to meet at such time and place as he thinks fit, so statement 1 is correct. The same Article prescribes only that six months shall not intervene between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next; it lays down no number of sessions and no minimum number of sitting days. The three sessions held each year - Budget, Monsoon and Winter - are a matter of convention, not of constitutional provision, so statement 2 is wrong and statement 3 is right.

items.value: Only pairs 2 and 3 are correctly matched - Banian as the Company's Indian agent and Mirasidar as the designated revenue payer
items.reasoning: A banian was the Indian broker, agent and money-lender attached to a European trading house or to a servant of the East India Company, so pair 2 is right. Mirasidars were the hereditary landholders of the Tamil country who held mirasi right in the village and were the recognised payers of revenue to the State, so pair 3 is right. An aurang was not an officer at all but a place - the warehouse or depot at which the Company's textiles were collected from the weavers before shipment - so pairing it with charge of the treasury is wrong.

items.value: Statements 2 and 3 are correct - the Lokottaravadins branched from the Mahasanghikas, whose deification of the Buddha fed Mahayana; the Sthaviravadins are not Mahayana
items.reasoning: The great schism divided the sangha into the Sthaviravadins, the Elders, from whom the Theravada line descends, and the Mahasanghikas; Sthaviravada therefore belongs to the older Hinayana tradition and not to Mahayana, so statement 1 is wrong. The Lokottaravadins, who held that the Buddha was lokottara or transcendent, were an offshoot of the Mahasanghikas, so statement 2 is correct, and it was precisely this exaltation of the Buddha above ordinary humanity that supplied Mahayana with its transcendent Buddha and its Bodhisattva ideal, so statement 3 is correct.

items.value: The Industrial Revolution ruined Indian handicrafts in the first half of the nineteenth century
items.reasoning: Cheap machine-made British yarn and cloth flooded Indian markets in these decades while Indian manufactures faced prohibitive duties in Britain, and the result was the de-industrialisation that destroyed the livelihood of weavers and other artisans. The other options belong to a later period or are simply false: the first modern Indian textile mill was set up at Bombay only in 1854 and the first railway line ran in 1853, while colonial policy kept duties on British imports low rather than heavy.

items.value: The correct order is 2 - 4 - 1 - 3: Mahendravarman I, then Gopala, then Bhoja, then Parantaka I
items.reasoning: Mahendravarman I established Pallava power in the early seventh century, about 600 to 630. Gopala founded the Pala dynasty about 750. Mihira Bhoja, under whom the Gurjara-Pratiharas rose to their height, reigned in the ninth century, about 836 to 885. Parantaka I, who consolidated Chola power after Vijayalaya, ruled about 907 to 955. The sequence from earliest to latest is therefore 2, 4, 1, 3.

items.value: A hundi was a bill of exchange
items.reasoning: A hundi was a written instrument directing one party to pay a named sum to another - an indigenous bill of exchange by which merchants and bankers transferred money and extended credit over long distances without moving coin, and which could be endorsed and discounted. It was a commercial credit instrument, not a royal advisory, an account book or a feudal order.
